title: The Four Weepings of the Garments of the First Man
arc: The teaching traces four weepings of the Five Sons of the First Man — three at the descent into the mingled state, when they saw the Darkness and foreknew their captivity, and a fourth, heavier weeping at the consummation, when the Last Andrias gathers the redeemed and those souls who loved the Darkness are sealed away from rest forever.
reading:
This chapter sets the whole drama of redemption between two weepings — one at the beginning of the cosmos and one at its end — and explains why the second is heavier than the first.

The "garments" or "sons of the First Man" are the five attributes of Divine Truth that the First Man bears with him in his descent: the Five Sons, the Five Storehouses, the living-soul substance which becomes the elemental fabric of the cosmos. They are simultaneously his children (born of him) and his clothing (the form in which he is borne into ultimates). When the teaching speaks of their weeping, it is describing the grief proper to Divine Truth itself as it accommodates downward into the natural to engage the proprium.

The first three weepings belong to the descent. When the Sons "saw the Darkness, the Enemy, hanging extended at a distance against them," they perceived in advance everything that would befall them — the whole long captivity of light bound in matter, every assault, every degradation. They knew what would rise up against them and come upon them through the King of Darkness. They wept three times — three being the fullness of process, the complete cycle of the descent foreseen as a complete suffering — and then fell silent. The silence is not consolation but the acceptance of Necessity: bound by the requirement of redemption, they hastened in toward the Enemy. The weeping ends because the descent must be carried out, and grief at the threshold gives way to the work itself. This is the inner pattern of accommodation: Divine Truth foresees the cost of entering the mingled state, mourns it, and then enters silently because the redemption of the Living Soul cannot otherwise be accomplished.

The fourth weeping belongs to the consummation. At the chosen moment when the Last Andrias goes forth — when the gathering-statue of all redeemed light is finally formed and rises — there are souls who do not enter it. These are the souls "prepared for the Error according to their works": those who, by what they have desired and loved, have made themselves over to the Darkness. At the consummation they are separated forth from the Last Andrias; they are bound with the Darkness in exact correspondence to the way they desired it, hour by hour, loving it and setting it before them. They are cut off from the unity of the great Andrias and remain behind forever. No rest reaches them from that moment onward. This is the eschatological binding — the bolos, the final compacted state of evil — described from the side of those mourning it.

The mourners of this fourth weeping are named: "the firmaments of the elements," that is, the very garments of the First Man considered as the fixed boundaries by which the elemental order has been held. Because they are the substance of Divine Truth gone out into the cosmos, they grieve over the souls who, having been offered redemption through them, refuse it and so are cut off from rest. Their weeping is heavier than the first three because in the first three the grief had a term — the descent could be completed, the captives could be raised — but in this fourth weeping the grief is over what is irrevocable. There is no further salvation that can reach those who are bound with the Darkness they loved; consequently the grief itself does not cease.

The spiritual teaching is therefore double. First, it shows that the descent of Divine Truth into the natural is itself a form of suffering foreseen and undertaken — the Lord does not enter the mingled state lightly, but with full knowledge of what the proprium will do to his garments, and he goes in only because Necessity (the rescue of the Living Soul) requires it. Second, it shows that at the consummation a separation is fixed: those who have shaped themselves to the Darkness by their loves and works become inseparable from it, and the divine order itself registers this loss as an unending grief. The four weepings together map the entire arc of redemption — three for the descent and labor, one for the final sorting — and the asymmetry between them, three completed and one without end, conveys the gravity of the consummation: the work of redemption closes for those who are gathered, but the grief over those who remain behind does not close.
